blocks.content: Caching is storing the result of an expensive operation in a fast storage layer so the next request returns it instantly. In this topic we go deeper how you actually put caching into a system: the patterns, the strategies, eviction policies, invalidation, and the problems that come up at scale.
The fundamentals: hit vs miss, TTL, and why it works are covered in the previous topic. Here we focus on how to design a caching layer properly.
Caching patterns: how the cache fits in the flow
blocks.text: Caching patterns: how the cache fits in the flow

blocks.content: The pattern defines who reads and writes the cache, and in what order relative to the database. There are four main patterns and each makes a different trade-off.
1. Cache-aside (lazy loading)
The application manages the cache. On a read, check the cache first. On a miss, fetch from DB, store in cache, return. The cache is only populated when data is actually requested never eagerly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279633164-421868869.png
blocks.alt: App checks cache first, on a miss queries the DB and populates the cache

blocks.content: App receives request and first checks Redis cache.

["If data is found, it returns immediately.
","If not found, it queries the database.
"]
items: If data is found, it returns immediately.
If not found, it queries the database.

blocks.content: After getting data, it stores it in cache with TTL. Then returns the response. Next requests for same data are served from cache instead of DB.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124480-711001671.png
Use when: reads are far more frequent than writes. The default pattern for most caching use cases user profiles, product pages, API responses.
2. Write through
Every write goes to the cache and the database simultaneously. The cache is always in sync with the DB. Reads always hit the cache no misses for data that has been written.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124481-972645239.png
App writes data to cache first. Cache then writes the same data to database. All reads go to cache, not database.
Since cache is always updated, reads always hit cache. This is write-through caching. It keeps cache and DB consistent but adds write latency.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279636227-601415176.png
blocks.alt: App writes go through the cache to the database synchronously before being confirmed

blocks.content: Use when: data is written and read frequently and you can't tolerate staleness. Works well combined with cache-aside write-through on updates, cache-aside on reads.
3. Write-behind (write-back)
Writes go to the cache only the DB is updated asynchronously in the background. Writes feel instant to the application. The cache is the primary store; the DB is eventually consistent.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124481-729322547.png
App writes data to cache first and returns immediately. Cache pushes the write to a queue. Worker processes the queue and updates the database later. Reads always come from cache so they are fast.
This is write-back or write-behind caching. It improves write performance but DB is eventually consistent.
If the cache crashes before the background worker flushes to DB, data is lost. Write-behind trades durability for speed only use it when losing recent writes is acceptable.
Use when: write performance is critical and you can tolerate eventual consistency. Common in gaming (leaderboards), analytics counters, and social media like counts.
4. Read-through
The cache itself fetches from the DB on a miss the application only ever talks to the cache. The cache library or a cache proxy handles the miss logic transparently.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124481-393024343.png
App sends request to cache.

["If cache hit, response is returned immediately.
","If cache miss, cache calls a loader.
"]
items: If cache hit, response is returned immediately.
If cache miss, cache calls a loader.

blocks.content: Loader fetches data from database. Result is returned and stored in cache. Then response is sent back. Next requests will hit cache instead of DB.
Use when: you want to keep caching logic out of your application code entirely. Popular with ORM-level caches and managed cache services like AWS ElastiCache with read-through support.
5. Patterns at a glance
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124482-221491921.png
6. Cache invalidation strategies
When data changes, the cached copy becomes stale. Invalidation is how you handle that. There is no perfect strategy each one trades consistency against complexity.
1. TTL expiry ( passive invalidation )
Let the entry expire naturally. Accept a window of staleness equal to the TTL. Zero extra logic needed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019243-397272418.png
blocks.alt: TTL expiry removes an entry automatically once its time-to-live elapses

blocks.content: App reads data from cache first.
If cache entry is still within TTL, it is valid and returned immediately.
If TTL has expired, cache treats it as a miss.
Then system fetches fresh data from the database.
Fresh data is returned to the user.
At the same time, it is stored back in cache with a new TTL.
This keeps data reasonably fresh while still getting cache performance benefits.
2. Delete on write ( active invalidation )
When data is updated in the DB, immediately delete the cached key. The next read is a miss and fetches fresh data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279640566-341528711.png
blocks.alt: On a write, the DB is updated first and the cache key is deleted right after

blocks.content: App first updates the database with the latest data so the source of truth is always correct.
Right after updating, it deletes the corresponding cache entry to avoid serving stale data.
Now the cache does not have that key anymore.
When the next read request comes, it goes to cache but results in a miss.
Since cache missed, the system fetches fresh data from the database.
This fresh data is returned to the user.
At the same time, the data is stored back in cache for future requests.
Subsequent reads will now hit the cache and be fast again.
This pattern is called cache invalidation and ensures strong consistency with slightly slower first read after update.
3. Event-driven invalidation
Services publish change events. Any service with a cached copy of that data listens and invalidates on the event. Decoupled and scalable but more infrastructure.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279642197-185663916.png
blocks.alt: A service publishes a change event and other services invalidate their cached copies

blocks.content: Service A updates the database with new data.
After updating, it publishes an event to the event bus saying data has changed.
Other services like Service B and Service C listen to this event.
When they receive the notification, they invalidate or delete their cache entries.
This ensures all services remove stale data from their caches.
On the next read, each service will fetch fresh data from the database and update its cache.
This pattern keeps multiple caches in sync across services using events.
7. Eviction policies
When the cache is full and a new entry needs space, the eviction policy decides what gets removed. This is separate from TTL expiry eviction is space-driven, TTL is time-driven.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024006-97951447.png
blocks.alt: When the cache is full, the eviction policy chooses a victim before inserting the new entry

blocks.content: Eviction happens when cache is full and needs space, it decides which data to remove.

["LRU removes the data that was not used for the longest time, assuming recently used data is more important.
","LFU removes the data with the least number of accesses, keeping frequently used data safe.
","FIFO removes the oldest inserted data, without caring if it is still popular.
","Random removes any entry randomly, simple and sometimes effective when access pattern is uniform.
"]
items: LRU removes the data that was not used for the longest time, assuming recently used data is more important.
LFU removes the data with the least number of accesses, keeping frequently used data safe.
FIFO removes the oldest inserted data, without caring if it is still popular.
Random removes any entry randomly, simple and sometimes effective when access pattern is uniform.

blocks.content: TTL is time based expiry, eviction is space based removal.
8. Cache stampede and how to fix it
blocks.text: 8. Cache stampede and how to fix it

blocks.content: When a popular key expires, dozens or hundreds of concurrent requests all get a cache miss and all race to the database simultaneously. The DB gets a sudden spike of identical queries.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279653447-29914171.png
blocks.alt: When a popular key expires, many concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once

blocks.content: Popular product page cached for 5 min. TTL expires. 300 concurrent users hit the page. All 300 get a cache miss. All 300 query the DB. DB goes from 2 queries/min to 300 in under a second.
Many requests come at the same time for the same data. Cache does not have the data yet, so all requests see a miss.
Each request independently goes to the database. Instead of 1 DB query, hundreds of queries hit the DB together.

["This sudden spike overloads the database.
","This problem is called cache stampede.
"]
items: This sudden spike overloads the database.
This problem is called cache stampede.

blocks.content: It happens when cache is empty or expired and many requests hit at once.
Alternative fix probabilistic early expiry
Instead of waiting for TTL to fully expire, the system starts refreshing data slightly before expiry.
When a request comes, it checks how much time is left for that cache entry.
If the entry is near expiry, only some requests randomly trigger a refresh.
Most requests still get the old cached value, so no sudden DB spike happens.
A small percentage of requests recompute the data and update the cache in advance. This spreads the refresh load over time instead of all requests hitting DB at once.
As a result, cache never fully expires for hot data and stampede is avoided.
9. Cache warming ( avoiding cold start )
A fresh cache has zero entries. Every request is a miss. The DB gets hammered until the cache fills up. Cache warming pre-populates the cache before traffic arrives.
Before the server starts, the system preloads important data into cache.

["It fetches top products and stores them in Redis with TTL.
","It also fetches most active users and caches them.
"]
items: It fetches top products and stores them in Redis with TTL.
It also fetches most active users and caches them.

blocks.content: This ensures frequently accessed data is already in cache. When traffic starts, requests hit cache instead of DB. This avoids cold start and prevents sudden load on database.
It improves performance from the very first request.
10. Distributed cache vs local cache
When you have multiple application servers, you have a choice: cache locally on each server, or share a single cache across all of them.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024005-433675606.png
blocks.alt: Local cache lives in each server process memory and is not shared across servers

blocks.content: Local cache is inside application memory so it is extremely fast with no network call.
Each server has its own cache so data is not shared.
This causes inconsistency because one server may have data while another does not.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279671311-278770015.png
blocks.alt: A distributed cache like Redis is shared across all application servers

blocks.content: Distributed cache like Redis is shared across all servers. It requires a network call so slightly slower.
All servers use the same cache so data is consistent. This works better when scaling multiple servers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124482-968525490.png
